questions.stem: In the presence of an inhibitor, an enzyme's Lineweaver–Burk plot shows the same y-intercept but an x-intercept closer to zero. What type of inhibitor is it?
questions.explanation: Same y-intercept = unchanged Vmax; x-intercept (−1/Km) closer to zero = increased Km → competitive. A: Non-competitive raises the y-intercept (↓Vmax) with the same x-intercept. C: Uncompetitive gives parallel lines (both change). D: Irreversible inhibition lowers Vmax. E: An activator wouldn't raise Km.

questions.stem: Blood glucose is ~5 mM between meals. Hexokinase has a Km for glucose of ~0.05 mM and glucokinase ~6 mM. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Glucokinase works near Vmax between meals
options.B: Both work at about half Vmax
options.C: Hexokinase has lower affinity for glucose
options.D: Glucokinase is mainly found in erythrocytes
options.E: Hexokinase works near Vmax between meals

questions.explanation: With [S] ≫ Km (5 vs 0.05 mM), hexokinase is saturated. A: Glucokinase, at [S] below its Km, runs well below Vmax and speeds up as glucose rises after meals. B: Only glucokinase is near half Vmax. C: Hexokinase has the lower Km, so higher affinity. D: Glucokinase is hepatic; RBCs use hexokinase.

questions.stem: Which statement about enzymes as catalysts is correct?

options.C: They lower the activation energy without changing equilibrium
options.D: They are consumed in the reaction
options.E: Their active sites are most complementary to the substrate's ground state

questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy; equilibrium and ΔG are unchanged and the enzyme is regenerated. A: ΔG is unaffected. B: Equilibrium is unaffected. D: Enzymes aren't consumed. E: Active sites best fit the transition state.

questions.stem: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex. How do apparent Km and Vmax change?
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Vmax and apparent Km (binding ES pulls the equilibrium toward ES). B: That's competitive. C: That's pure non-competitive. D: Inhibitors don't raise Vmax. E: Binding ES necessarily changes kinetics.

questions.stem: A regulatory enzyme gives a sigmoidal velocity vs [S] curve and is inhibited by the final product of its pathway. Which terms best describe it?
questions.explanation: Sigmoidal kinetics = allosteric (usually multisubunit) enzyme; end-product inhibition = feedback inhibition. A: Michaelis–Menten enzymes give hyperbolic curves. C: Zymogens are inactive precursors. D: Isozymes are different proteins catalyzing the same reaction. E: Allosteric enzymes are usually multimeric.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man of East Asian descent develops facial flushing, tachycardia, and nausea after half a glass of wine. Which enzyme variant best explains this?
questions.explanation: Lacking the low-Km (high-affinity) ALDH2 lets acetaldehyde accumulate, causing flushing. A: Low ADH activity would reduce acetaldehyde formation. B: CYP2E1 induction doesn't explain acute flushing. C: Catalase is a minor ethanol pathway. E: Glucokinase is unrelated.

questions.stem: A farmer arrives 12 hours after organophosphate pesticide exposure with salivation, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations. Atropine reduces the secretions, but pralidoxime has no effect. Why?

options.A: Organophosphates are reversible inhibitors that have washed out
options.B: Pralidoxime works only by blocking muscarinic receptors
options.C: Organophosphates block acetylcholine synthesis, not breakdown
options.D: Atropine has already reactivated the enzyme
options.E: The phosphorylated AChE has aged and is permanently inhibited

questions.explanation: Organophosphates phosphorylate the catalytic serine of AChE (irreversible inhibition). Pralidoxime removes the phosphate only before the adduct "ages"; after that, recovery waits on new enzyme over weeks, while atropine still blocks muscarinic effects. A: They are irreversible, covalent inhibitors. B: Blocking muscarinic receptors is atropine's action. C: They block ACh breakdown, so ACh accumulates. D: Atropine is a receptor blocker and doesn't act on AChE.

questions.stem: FAD stays tightly bound to its enzyme throughout catalysis, whereas NAD⁺ binds, is reduced and dissociates. How are these coenzymes classified?
questions.explanation: Coenzymes that associate permanently are prosthetic groups (FAD); those that associate transiently are co-substrates (NAD⁺). A: Reversed. B: Both are organic, vitamin-derived coenzymes, not metal ions. C: The apoenzyme is the protein part; the holoenzyme is protein plus cofactor. E: Allosteric effectors bind a separate site to regulate activity; these take part in the reaction.
